title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
Chapter 7 defines the sample that Part II of Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016) uses from here on: the monthly universe of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP. Before any predictive variable is studied, the chapter asks what this universe contains, decomposing it by stock exchange and by industry, in terms of both the number of stocks and their aggregate market value. It then defines the monthly stock return, explains how delistings are handled, and introduces the excess return that serves as the dependent variable in essentially every later analysis.
The second half of the chapter turns from individual stocks to the market as a whole. It chooses a proxy for the market portfolio, the Fama–French \(MKT\) factor, and examines its long-run reward and risk. Together, the sample definition, the return definition, and the market factor are the foundation on which the CAPM risk model and the cross-sectional analyses of the following chapters are built. This page follows the chapter’s own order and places the replicated figures and tables next to the book’s discussion.

title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
1.1 Sample Definition
For each month \(t\), the sample consists of every security in CRSP’s monthly stock names file whose name record is in force on the last day of the month and whose share code identifies a U.S.-based common stock:
\[
NAMEDT \leq \text{month-end of } t \leq NAMEENDT ,
\qquad
SHRCD \in \{10, 11\} .
\]
The first digit of SHRCD (1) marks an ordinary common share; the second digit (0 or 1) marks a firm incorporated in the United States. Exchange is not a condition: stocks on other exchanges, or with no exchange information, remain in the sample and are only separated out when the composition is examined.
The choice of the month-end rather than “any time during the month” is deliberate. Every analysis in Part II measures a predictive variable at the end of month \(t\) and relates it to the stock’s return in month \(t+1\). An investor deciding at the end of month \(t\) can only choose among the stocks that exist at that moment, so the sample is defined to coincide with that investment universe. A stock that was delisted mid-month is not available to that investor and is correctly excluded; a stock listed mid-month is available and is correctly included.
names = pl.read_parquet(RAW / "ch07_msenames.parquet").filter(pl.col("shrcd").is_in([10, 11]))
names = names.with_columns(nd=to_date("namedt"), ne=to_date("nameendt").fill_null(date(9999, 12, 31)))

M0, M1 = 1925 * 12 + 11, 2012 * 12 + 11
sample = (
    names.with_columns(
        m0=pl.max_horizontal(midx(pl.col("nd")), M0),
        m1=pl.min_horizontal(midx(pl.col("ne")) - (pl.col("ne") != pl.col("ne").dt.month_end()).cast(pl.Int32), M1),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("m0") <= pl.col("m1"))
    .with_columns(m=pl.int_ranges("m0", pl.col("m1") + 1))
    .explode("m", empty_as_null=False)
    .with_columns(ym=((pl.col("m") // 12) * 100 + pl.col("m") % 12 + 1).cast(pl.Int32))
    .select("permno", "ym", "exchcd", "siccd")
)
The implementation expands each valid CRSP name interval into the month-end observations it covers. A name record starting on NAMEDT first covers the end of that same month; it last covers the end of the month of NAMEENDT only if NAMEENDT falls on that month’s final day, and otherwise the preceding month-end. Name records for one PERMNO never overlap, so each stock appears at most once per month, which the script verifies.

title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
2.1 Market Capitalization
\[
MktCap_{i,t} = \frac{\lvert ALTPRC_{i,t} \times SHROUT_{i,t} \rvert}{1000}
\]
SHROUT is the number of shares outstanding in thousands and ALTPRC the month-end price, so the ratio is in millions of dollars. ALTPRC is used rather than PRC because PRC is missing or zero when a stock neither trades nor is quoted on the last trading day, whereas ALTPRC falls back to the last available price. When there is no trade, CRSP stores the bid–ask midpoint with a negative sign, which the absolute value removes. If either field is missing, market capitalization is missing. Figures 7.2 and 7.4 report values in billions of CPI-adjusted December 2012 dollars.
    .with_columns(mktcap=(pl.col("altprc") * pl.col("shrout")).abs() / 1000)
base = cpi.filter(pl.col("ym") == END)["cpi"][0]
sample = (
    sample.join(msf, on=["permno", "ym"], how="left")
    .join(cpi, on="ym", how="left")
    .with_columns(mktcap_r=pl.col("mktcap") * base / pl.col("cpi"))
)
The first line is the book’s definition; the second block rescales each month’s value by the ratio of the December 2012 CPI to that month’s CPI, so that a dollar of market value in 1926 and in 2012 carry the same purchasing power. Without this adjustment the early part of the sample would be invisible on a chart dominated by recent nominal values.

Figure 7.1 — Number of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Exchange

For its first four decades the CRSP universe is essentially the NYSE. The sample grows slowly from about five hundred stocks in December 1925 to a little over a thousand by mid-1962, nearly all of them NYSE-listed. The series then shows two discontinuities that have nothing to do with the economy and everything to do with database coverage. In July 1962 AMEX stocks enter the CRSP file and the count jumps by roughly 800 in one month. In December 1972 NASDAQ stocks enter, and the count roughly doubles again. From there the universe expands through the 1980s and 1990s, peaks in November 1997 at about 7,500 stocks, and then contracts steadily; by December 2012 the sample has fallen by roughly half, to 3,742 stocks in the replication.
The July 1962 break explains a convention that runs through the entire empirical literature. Many predictive variables need one year of prior data, so the first month in which AMEX stocks can be used is June 1963. This is why most studies, and Part II of the book from Section 7.2.1 onward, begin their sample in June 1963 (return months from July 1963).


Figure 7.2 — Value of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Exchange

The number of listed stocks and their economic importance are not the same thing. The AMEX inclusion of July 1962 raised the stock count by about three-quarters, but the aggregate market value of the sample rose by only a few percent: the newly added stocks were numerous and small. The same holds for NASDAQ in December 1972, when more than half of the stocks in the sample but only about 13% of its value were NASDAQ-listed.
Historically, the value of the CRSP universe has been NYSE value. NASDAQ’s share becomes substantial only from the 1990s and peaks during the dot-com period, when it approaches 36% of the total in March 2000, the month in which the sample’s total real value also peaks. AMEX and the Other group never account for a meaningful share of market value at any point in the sample.

IND = [
    (1, 999, "Agriculture, forestry, and fishing"),
    (1000, 1499, "Mining"),
    (1500, 1799, "Construction"),
    (2000, 3999, "Manufacturing"),
    (4000, 4999, "Transportation, communications, electric, gas, and sanitary services"),
    (5000, 5199, "Wholesale trade"),
    (5200, 5999, "Retail trade"),
    (6000, 6799, "Finance, insurance, and real estate"),
    (7000, 8999, "Services"),
    (9000, 9999, "Public administration"),
]
IND = [(lo, hi, full.split(",")[0].split(" ")[0], full) for lo, hi, full in IND]
IND_COLS = [short for _, _, short, _ in IND] + ["Missing"]
ind = pl.lit("Missing")
for lo, hi, name, _ in reversed(IND):
    ind = pl.when(pl.col("siccd").is_between(lo, hi)).then(pl.lit(name)).otherwise(ind)
sample = sample.with_columns(exch=exch, ind=ind)
The list is Table 7.1 verbatim, and the loop builds one nested when/then expression from it, so every stock-month receives the division whose range contains its SICCD and “Missing” otherwise. The book states the rule for zero; SIC codes that fall between the divisions (for example 1800–1999) have no book rule and are also placed in “Missing”, an implementation choice that affects very few observations.


Figure 7.3 — Number of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Industry

Manufacturing firms are the largest group in every month of the sample, and in the early decades they are the majority: the book reports that their share peaks above two-thirds in June 1946, which the replication reproduces exactly (583 of 864 stocks). The later sample looks different in kind. From the 1980s on, finance and services grow into the second and third largest groups, and by the late 1990s the two combined approach the manufacturing count.
The December 1972 jumps in several industries are not economic events. They are the NASDAQ coverage expansion of Figure 7.1 seen through the industry lens: the newly added NASDAQ firms were concentrated in finance and in firms without a usable industry code. The book reports that agriculture jumps from 87 to 810 stocks and finance from 247 to 748 in that month. The replication reproduces the finance count exactly, but the agriculture jump does not appear; instead the “Missing” group jumps to 719 stocks. This is consistent with placeholder SIC codes in the book’s data vintage having since been reset to zero, though the book gives no detail that would confirm the mechanism. The lesson for sample-composition work is the same either way: a break in an industry series should be checked against database coverage before it is read as a change in the economy.


Figure 7.4 — Value of Stocks in CRSP Sample by Industry

Figure 7.3 counts firms, whereas Figure 7.4 weights their economic importance by market value. On this measure manufacturing is even more dominant than by count, and the picture is more stable: the entry of many small NASDAQ firms in 1972 barely registers in value terms. Finance becomes the clear second industry by value only in the 2000s, later than it does by count, because many of the financial firms added in the 1970s and 1980s were small.
The dot-com period is where the value and count pictures diverge most. The transportation division, which includes communications, and the services division, which includes software and internet firms, rise sharply in real value through the late 1990s and give most of it back after March 2000. The same reversal is visible in finance around 2008. These are the industry components of the market-wide drawdowns that Section 5 examines.

title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
3.1 Monthly Stock Returns
The monthly return is the RET field of CRSP’s monthly stock file: the return from the last trade of the previous month to the last trade of the current month, including distributions. For the vast majority of stock-months this is the return an investor would have realized, and it is used unchanged. The exception is the month in which a stock is delisted. The last trade price recorded in that month is not necessarily the value the investor ends up with, because the investor is typically still holding the stock when it leaves the exchange.

title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
3.2 Delisting Adjustment
Delistings are often unexpected and leave no time to trade out of the position, so a return series that stops at the last exchange trade would overstate what investors earned, particularly for stocks removed for financial distress. CRSP’s delisting file records the delisting date (DLSTDT), a reason code (DLSTCD), and, when CRSP can determine a post-delisting value, the delisting return (DLRET). When DLRET is missing the book follows Shumway (1997) and imputes a return from the reason code:







Month \(t+1\)
Return used




No delisting
CRSP RET


Delisting, DLRET available
DLRET


Delisting, DLRET missing, DLSTCD in {500, 520, 551–573, 574, 580, 584}
−30%


Delisting, DLRET missing, other DLSTCD
−100%



These are the specific delisting codes for which the book assigns a −30% return when DLRET is unavailable. They are not a single category: the list includes codes for a price below the exchange minimum, insufficient capital or float, and bankruptcy, but also for a move to over-the-counter trading, delisting at the company’s request, liquidation, going private, and “reason unavailable”. All other codes receive −100%.






ImportantReplacement, not compounding



The book “take[s] the return of the stock to be the delisting return.” In a delisting month the delisting return replaces the month’s return; it is not compounded with RET as \((1+RET)(1+DLRET)-1\).


BAD = pl.col("dlstcd").is_in([500, 520, 574, 580, 584]) | pl.col("dlstcd").is_between(551, 573)
dl = (
    pl.read_parquet(RAW / "ch07_msedelist.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("dlstcd") > 199)
    .with_columns(ym=ym_of(to_date("dlstdt")))
    .with_columns(
        dlfill=pl.when(pl.col("dlret").is_not_null()).then(pl.col("dlret"))
               .when(BAD).then(-0.30).otherwise(-1.00),
        how=pl.when(pl.col("dlret").is_not_null()).then(pl.lit("dlret"))
            .when(BAD).then(pl.lit("-30%")).otherwise(pl.lit("-100%")),
    )
    .select("permno", "ym", "dlstcd", "dlret", "dlfill", "how")
)
BAD is the book’s list of −30% codes. For each delisting event the code produces dlfill, the return that will be used in the delisting month: DLRET when CRSP has one, and the imputed value otherwise. The adjusted return is then obtained by taking dlfill where it exists and RET elsewhere, which is the coalesce in the next code block. The filter on DLSTCD is an implementation choice, not a Chapter 7 rule: CRSP’s codes in the 100s denote securities that are still active rather than delisted.

title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
3.3 Excess Returns and Timing
Four return variables are used in Tables 7.2 and 7.3. With \(RF_{t+1}\) the monthly return on the risk-free security from Kenneth French’s data library,
\[
\begin{aligned}
RET_{i,t+1} &: \text{CRSP } RET \text{, unadjusted} &
ret_{i,t+1} &= RET_{i,t+1} - RF_{t+1} \\
R_{i,t+1}   &: \text{delisting-adjusted return} &
r_{i,t+1}   &= R_{i,t+1} - RF_{t+1}
\end{aligned}
\]
all recorded in percent. The timing is the one described in Section 1.1:
end of month t          sample membership; predictive variables measured here
        ↓
month t+1               the stock's return, R_{i,t+1}, and excess return, r_{i,t+1}
Within one month’s cross section the same \(RF_{t+1}\) is subtracted from every stock, so raw and excess returns rank stocks identically and any cross-sectional pattern in one is a pattern in the other. The distinction matters in the time series: the risk-free rate varies over time, and a factor regression of returns rather than excess returns would let that variation contaminate the intercept. Since the intercept of such regressions is usually the object of interest, the book works with excess returns throughout, and \(r_{i,t+1}\) is the focal return variable of Part II.
panel = (
    sample.filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(T0, T1)).select("permno", "ym")
    .with_columns(ym1=ym_shift(pl.col("ym"), 1))
    .join(ret, left_on=["permno", "ym1"], right_on=["permno", "ym"], how="left")
    .join(dl, left_on=["permno", "ym1"], right_on=["permno", "ym"], how="left")
    .join(ff, left_on="ym1", right_on="ym", how="left")
    .with_columns(R=pl.coalesce("dlfill", "RET"))
    .with_columns(
        RET=pl.col("RET") * 100, R=pl.col("R") * 100,
        ret=(pl.col("RET") - pl.col("rf")) * 100, r=(pl.col("R") - pl.col("rf")) * 100,
    )
)
Each stock-month of the sample at \(t\) is given the key of the following month and joined left to the return, delisting, and risk-free tables at \(t+1\). The left join is what keeps the delisting adjustment meaningful: a stock that is in the sample at the end of \(t\) and delists during \(t+1\) stays in the cross section with its delisting return, whereas an inner join on the stocks alive at \(t+1\) would silently remove exactly the observations that Shumway’s adjustment exists to keep.

Three features of the distribution carry over to everything that follows.
Positive skewness. In the average month the mean excess return is positive while the median is slightly negative, and the cross-sectional skewness is strongly positive. The asymmetry is structural: a stock cannot lose more than 100%, so the excess return is bounded below by roughly \(-100\% - RF\), but there is no corresponding bound above. A typical stock earns a little less than the risk-free rate in a typical month; the positive mean comes from a minority of large winners.
Fat tails. The average excess kurtosis is far above the value of zero that a normal distribution would give. The monthly cross section routinely contains returns of several hundred percent and of close to −100%, and the 5th and 95th percentiles sit at roughly ±20%. Any method that assumes normal returns, or that is sensitive to extreme values, has to contend with this.
Effect of the delisting adjustment. The adjusted and unadjusted distributions are similar in the middle: percentiles from the 5th to the 95th differ by hundredths of a percent. The adjustment acts in the tails. It lowers the mean slightly by adding many returns of −30% and −100%, makes the average minimum more negative, and, because some delisting returns are very large, raises the average maximum and with it the standard deviation and kurtosis. The book concludes that the choice rarely changes empirical results, but uses the adjusted return because it is closer to what an investor realizes.
In the replication the unadjusted rows (\(ret\), \(RET\)) reproduce the book to the second decimal on almost every statistic, and the adjusted rows reproduce the mean and every percentile from the 5th to the 95th. The adjusted standard deviation, kurtosis, and maximum are lower than the book’s. The discrepancy is thus concentrated in the delisting-adjusted tail statistics, and since the adjusted and unadjusted rows differ only in the delisting returns, delisting-return observations are the likely source. Confirming whether this reflects CRSP data-vintage revisions would require a record-level comparison with the book’s data vintage.

The post-1963 sample is a different universe rather than a shorter one. It contains on average about half again as many stocks per month, because the years with only NYSE coverage are gone and AMEX and NASDAQ stocks are present throughout. The inclusion of AMEX and NASDAQ materially changes the cross-sectional return distribution, which becomes wider and more heavy-tailed: the cross-sectional standard deviation, the skewness, the excess kurtosis, and the average maximum are all higher, and the average minimum is closer to −100%. The average excess return is somewhat lower and the median more negative. The distribution that later chapters work with is thus wider and heavier-tailed than the full-history one.
The comparison with the book follows the pattern of Table 7.2: unadjusted statistics match to the second decimal, adjusted percentiles and means match, and the adjusted dispersion measures are somewhat lower in the current data.

title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
text:
5.1 Market Portfolio Proxy
In the CAPM the market portfolio is the value-weighted portfolio of all assets: stocks and bonds, but also real estate, private businesses, and human capital. That portfolio cannot be observed, and even the portfolio of all financial securities is beyond reach because many securities have no observable price. Empirical work therefore uses a proxy built from the securities traded on U.S. stock exchanges, whose prices are recorded every day.
The book compares two such proxies. The first is the value-weighted portfolio of U.S.-based common stocks in CRSP, that is, of the sample defined in Section 1; its excess return is the Fama–French market factor, \(MKT\). The second is the broader CRSP value-weighted index, which also contains securities that are not U.S. common stocks (foreign-incorporated firms, closed-end funds, and other share types) but excludes ADRs. Over July 1926 to December 2012 the two excess-return series have nearly identical means and standard deviations and a correlation of about 0.9995. The choice between them is immaterial, and the book uses \(MKT\) as the market proxy for the remainder of the text.

The annualized Sharpe ratio is the monthly mean over the monthly standard deviation times \(\sqrt{12}\), which assumes independent monthly returns. A premium of roughly 0.6% per month with a standard deviation of over 5% is a noisy reward: the market’s excess return in a single month is far more likely to be dominated by risk than by the premium, and the premium reveals itself only through compounding over decades.

title: Chapter 7 — The CRSP Sample and Market Factor
section: 5.3 Figure 7.5 — Cumulative Excess Returns of MKT
text:
5.3 Figure 7.5 — Cumulative Excess Returns of MKT
\[
\text{Compounded excess return}_t = 100 \times \Bigl[\prod_{s \le t}(1 + MKT_s) - 1\Bigr],
\qquad
\text{Cumulative log excess return}_t = 100 \times \sum_{s \le t} \ln(1 + MKT_s).
\]
mkt = (
    ff.filter(pl.col("ym").is_between(192607, 201212)).sort("ym")
    .with_columns(logret=(1 + pl.col("mktrf")).log(), wealth=(1 + pl.col("mktrf")).cum_prod())
    .with_columns(
        compound_excess=100 * (pl.col("wealth") - 1),
        cumulative_log_excess=100 * pl.col("logret").cum_sum(),
        drawdown=pl.col("wealth") / pl.col("wealth").cum_max() - 1,
        date=pl.date(pl.col("ym") // 100, pl.col("ym") % 100, 1).dt.month_end(),
    )
)
The compounded series is the cumulative product of one plus the monthly market excess return, expressed as a percentage gain; the log series is the running sum of the log of one plus the monthly excess return. wealth is the cumulative product itself and is reused below for the drawdown calculation.

The two series contain the same information, plotted on scales that answer different questions. The compounded series gives the level: the compounded excess-return index grows to about 145 times its initial level by December 2012, corresponding to a cumulative excess return of about 14,411%. But because that number is a level, equal percentage moves are drawn as ever larger vertical distances as the index grows, so the solid line makes the late sample look far more volatile than the early one and makes the 1929–1932 crash, the largest percentage loss in the sample, almost invisible. The log series removes that distortion: a 10% loss is the same vertical distance in 1930 as in 2008, which is why the dashed line shows the early crash as the deep trough it was.

Drawdowns are measured from the running high-water mark of the compounded series; recovery is the first month in which cumulative wealth again reaches the previous peak. The 1929 crash needed more than fifteen years to recover; the 1968 and 2000 episodes, each more than half of cumulative wealth, needed fourteen years and more than the twelve years remaining in the sample, respectively. October 1987, with a monthly excess return of about −23%, produced the smallest of the four drawdowns and the fastest recovery.
Figure 7.5 shows that a strongly positive long-run market premium can coexist with very large and long-lasting drawdowns. The premium is real, but an investor collects it only by holding through periods in which more than half of accumulated wealth disappears and is not recovered for a decade or more. In the CAPM, beta measures a stock’s exposure to variation in this market factor.

title: Chapter 1 — Preliminaries
text:
Overview
Chapter 1 of Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016) has no table to reproduce. It defines the methodologies sample, names the variables, and identifies the databases used throughout Part I. Correspondingly, ch01.py only connects to WRDS, downloads the raw tables, and stores them as Parquet under data/raw/. Sample construction and every variable calculation happen in Chapter 2.
Code blocks on this page are cut from ch01.py at render time.



1. Replication Workflow
Book definitions
      ↓
Identify required datasets
      ↓
Download raw data from WRDS        ← ch01.py
      ↓
Store data as Parquet files
      ↓
Construct annual samples and variables   (Chapter 2)
      ↓
Replicate empirical results              (Chapter 2 onward)



2. Sample Framework
The methodologies sample is a stock × year panel for \(1988 \leq t \leq 2012\). A stock belongs to the year-\(t\) cross section if it is a U.S.-based common stock in CRSP on December 31 of year \(t\), which in CRSP’s share-code classification means SHRCD 10 or 11. Both constants are set once and reused in every query.
START, END = 1988, 2012

COMMON = "shrcd in (10, 11)"
Exchange is not a sample condition (Chapter 7, Section 7.1.2); EXCHCD is kept only for diagnostics.



3. Data Requirements
Three sources are needed: CRSP, Compustat, and the Fama–French factor library. The tables below are downloaded once and referred to by name in the rest of the project.









Dataset
Source
Variables kept
Used for




msenames
CRSP
PERMNO, NAMEDT, NAMEENDT; SHRCD; EXCHCD; NCUSIP, CUSIP; TICKER, COMNAM
Sample membership


msf
CRSP
RET; SHROUT (thousands); ALTPRC
Market capitalization, monthly returns


dsf
CRSP
RET, PRC, SHROUT
Daily returns for beta


msedelist
CRSP
DLSTDT, DLSTCD, DLRET
Delisting adjustment


ff_daily
Fama–French
MKTRF, RF
Beta regression


ff_monthly
Fama–French
MKTRF, RF
Risk-free leg of the annual excess return

UGVKEY, UPERMNO, ULINKTYPE, USEDFLAG, ULINKDT, ULINKENDDT
CRSP–Compustat link (Section 11)


funda
Compustat
GVKEY, CUSIP, DATADATE, FYEAR; SEQ, CEQ, PSTK, PSTKRV, PSTKL, TXDB, ITCB, TXDITC; AT, LT
Book equity






4. Download Mechanics
The wrds package opens the connection, which prompts for credentials and Duo authentication, so the script is run by hand rather than from this page.
db = wrds.Connection()
Files go to data/raw/ as Parquet, which preserves types and reads quickly in Polars; the directory is excluded from version control under the WRDS license.
RAW = Path(__file__).parent / "data" / "raw"
RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
One helper runs a query, converts the pandas result to Polars, and writes Parquet, skipping any file that already exists. An interrupted run therefore resumes where it stopped.
def save(name, query):
    path = RAW / f"{name}.parquet"
    if path.exists():
        return
    df = pl.from_pandas(db.raw_sql(query))
    df.write_parquet(path)



5. CRSP Security Information
crsp.msenames, restricted to common stocks, supplies the name-record intervals that Chapter 2 tests against December 31 of each year:
\[
NAMEDT \leq \text{December 31 of year } t \leq NAMEENDT
\]
save("msenames", f"""
    select permno, namedt, nameendt, shrcd, exchcd, ncusip, cusip, ticker, comnam
    from crsp.msenames
    where {COMMON}
""")



6. Restricting Large CRSP Files
The price files are restricted to PERMNOs that have ever been U.S. common stocks, through a SQL fragment spliced into the later queries. This is a PERMNO-level restriction only: the December 31 rule is not applied at download time, because a beta for year \(t\) needs every trading day of that year.
PERMNOS = f"permno in (select permno from crsp.msenames where {COMMON})"



7. Fama–French Factors
Daily factors feed the beta regression \(R_{i,d} - R_{f,d} = \alpha_i + \beta_i (R_{m,d} - R_{f,d}) + \varepsilon_{i,d}\); monthly RF is compounded into the annual risk-free return. The WRDS copy is in decimal units (0.0029 = 0.29%).
save("ff_daily", f"""
    select date, mktrf, rf
    from ff.factors_daily
    where date between '{START}-01-01' and '{END + 1}-12-31'
""")

save("ff_monthly", f"""
    select date, mktrf, rf
    from ff.factors_monthly
    where date between '{START}-01-01' and '{END}-12-31'
""")



8. CRSP Monthly Stock Data
msf supplies ALTPRC and SHROUT for market capitalization and RET for the monthly returns compounded into the one-year-ahead return. ALTPRC is CRSP’s alternative month-end price, which falls back to the last available price when PRC is missing and otherwise equals it.
save("msf", f"""
    select permno, date, ret, shrout, altprc
    from crsp.msf
    where date between '{START - 1}-01-01' and '{END + 1}-12-31'
      and {PERMNOS}
""")
Two boundary years deserve a note. The file starts at START - 1 (1987) because the book-to-market ratio attached to year \(t\) divides by December market capitalization of year \(t-1\) (Chapter 2, Section 3.5). It runs through END + 1 (2013), but that year is not used: the book’s data end in 2012, so the 2012 cross section has no one-year-ahead return, and Chapter 2 restricts the return calculation to 1989–2012.



9. Delisting Data
msedelist provides the delisting date, code, and return with which Chapter 2 replaces the return in a delisting month.
save("msedelist", """
    select permno, dlstdt, dlstcd, dlret
    from crsp.msedelist
""")



10. CRSP Daily Stock Data
The daily file exists solely for the beta estimation. It is downloaded one calendar year at a time, 1988 through 2013, skipping years already on disk, which keeps each WRDS query small and makes the download resumable.
(RAW / "dsf").mkdir(exist_ok=True)

for year in range(START, END + 2):
    path = RAW / "dsf" / f"dsf_{year}.parquet"
    if path.exists():
        continue

    df = pl.from_pandas(db.raw_sql(f"""
        select permno, date, ret, prc, shrout
        from crsp.dsf
        where date between '{year}-01-01' and '{year}-12-31'
          and {PERMNOS}
    """))
    df.write_parquet(path)



11. CRSP–Compustat Linking
CRSP (PERMNO) and Compustat (GVKEY) share no identifier. Following Chapter 10, Section 10.1, the bridge is CCM’s link-used table: links of type LU or LC with USEDFLAG 1, valid for a Compustat record whose DATADATE lies between ULINKDT and ULINKENDDT.
try:
    save("ccm_lnkused", """
        select ugvkey, upermno, ulinktype, ulinkprim, usedflag, ulinkdt, ulinkenddt
        from crsp.ccmxpf_lnkused
        where ulinktype in ('LU', 'LC') and usedflag = 1
    """)
except Exception as e:
    print(f"  ccm_lnkused  not available ({type(e).__name__}) - ch02 links by CUSIP only")






WarningCCM is not part of the WRDS subscription



The query fails with a permission error, which the try block catches. The link-used table was obtained separately as Parquet and placed at data/raw/ccm_lnkused.parquet, the path save() would have written, so the script skips it. Without that file Chapter 2 would fall back entirely to the book’s second method, matching CRSP NCUSIP to the first eight characters of the Compustat CUSIP; with it, the CUSIP match covers only firms the link table misses.





12. Compustat Fundamentals
comp.funda supplies the book-equity inputs of Chapter 10, Section 10.1: stockholders’ equity, deferred taxes, investment tax credit, and three measures of preferred stock. The where clause keeps the standard consolidated industrial format; INDL/STD are the book’s conditions, consol/popsrc the standard WRDS additions that make firm/date unique in the current file layout. The pull starts at START - 2 to leave room for fiscal-year timing.
save("funda", f"""
    select gvkey, cusip, datadate, fyear, seq, ceq, pstk, pstkrv, pstkl, txdb, itcb, txditc, at, lt
    from comp.funda
    where indfmt = 'INDL' and datafmt = 'STD'
      and popsrc = 'D' and consol = 'C'
      and datadate between '{START - 2}-01-01' and '{END}-12-31'
""")



13. Implementation Decisions
Key implementation choices and conventions used in the replication:








Decision
Choice
Reason




Sample period
1988–2012
Book, Chapter 1

SHRCD 10 or 11, no exchange filter
Book, Chapter 7


msf start year
1987, one year before the sample
BM for 1988 needs December 1987 market cap

2013, not used for returns
Kept in the download only


CRSP–Compustat link
CCM link-used table obtained outside WRDS, CUSIP fallback
Subscription lacks CCM

INDL/STD plus consol = 'C', popsrc = 'D'
Uniqueness of firm/date in the current file


Monthly price field
ALTPRC
Book, Chapter 7






Summary
ch01.py downloads the CRSP, Fama–French, and Compustat tables listed in Section 3 and stores them as Parquet; the raw files are the only input to Chapter 2.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing Replication
text:
This project is a chapter-by-chapter replication of
Bali, Engle, and Murray (2016),
Empirical Asset Pricing: The Cross Section of Stock Returns.
The objective is to reproduce the empirical procedures, variable construction, tables, and analyses presented throughout the book using the original or closely corresponding financial datasets.
Rather than reproducing only selected results, the project aims to reconstruct the empirical workflow of the book from data collection and sample construction through portfolio analysis, cross-sectional regressions, and other empirical asset-pricing applications.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing Replication
text:
1. Methodology
Identify the empirical procedure described in the book.
This includes:

sample definitions
variable definitions
timing conventions
estimation procedures
portfolio construction
regression specifications
summary statistics and other reported results

title: Empirical Asset Pricing Replication
text:
2. Data Construction
Construct the required variables from the underlying financial databases.
The implementation follows the definitions in the book as closely as possible.
When the book specifies a particular convention, that convention is preferred over alternative procedures commonly used in the literature.

3. Replication
Implement the empirical procedure in Python and reproduce the corresponding tables, statistics, or analyses.

Compare the replicated results with the values reported in the book.
Any meaningful differences are investigated and documented.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing Replication
text:
Follow the Book
The primary objective is replication rather than methodological modification.
Whenever the book explicitly specifies a procedure, the implementation follows that procedure as closely as possible.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing Replication
text:
Preserve Timing
Asset-pricing variables often depend critically on timing.
The replication therefore distinguishes carefully between:

formation periods
measurement periods
holding periods
future return periods

For example, a characteristic measured at time \(t\) may be used to explain or predict a return realized during \(t+1\).

title: Empirical Asset Pricing Replication
text:
Preserve Units
The units reported in the book are preserved whenever possible.
Examples include:

returns
market capitalization
accounting ratios
logarithmic transformations

Unit conversions are documented explicitly.

title: Empirical Asset Pricing Replication
text:
Avoid Unstated Adjustments
Transformations such as:

winsorization
trimming
additional exchange filters
missing-value replacement
alternative return adjustments

are not introduced unless they are supported by the book or required for a clearly documented implementation reason.

Some implementation details may not be fully specified in the book.
When an assumption is required, the project distinguishes between:

procedures explicitly stated in the book,
procedures inferred from the book’s methodology,
implementation decisions introduced for computational purposes.

title: Chapter 2 — Summary Statistics
text:
Chapter 2 introduces summary statistics on the methodologies sample. From the raw files of Chapter 1, ch02.py builds the annual stock-year sample, constructs Beta, MktCap, SIZE, BM, and the one-year-ahead excess return \(r\), and reproduces Table 2.1 (annual Beta statistics), Table 2.2 (their time-series average), and Table 2.3 (the same summary for every variable).
The script runs once and writes stock-level intermediates to data/interim/ and tables to output/tables/; this page reads those files, shows the relevant code cut from ch02.py at render time, and re-executes only a few short final steps.

title: Chapter 2 — Summary Statistics
text:
3.1 Beta
\(\beta_{i,t}\) is the slope of daily excess stock returns on daily excess market returns over calendar year \(t\), with at least 200 valid days:
\[
R_{i,d} - R_{f,d} = \alpha_{i,t} + \beta_{i,t}\,(R_{m,d} - R_{f,d}) + \varepsilon_{i,d}.
\]
Since a univariate OLS slope is a covariance over a variance, the script computes \(\operatorname{Cov}(R_{i,d}-R_{f,d},\,MKTRF_d)/\operatorname{Var}(MKTRF_d)\) directly with Polars aggregations; both moments use the same degrees-of-freedom convention, so the ratio is exact. Inputs are CRSP daily RET minus Fama–French daily RF, and MKTRF.
ff = pl.read_parquet(RAW / "ff_daily.parquet").with_columns(d=ymd("date"))

beta = (
    pl.scan_parquet(str(RAW / "dsf" / "*.parquet"))
    .join(KEEP.lazy(), on="permno", how="semi")
    .with_columns(d=ymd("date"))
    .join(ff.lazy().select("d", "mktrf", "rf"), on="d")
    .filter(pl.col("ret").is_finite())
    .with_columns(rx=pl.col("ret") - pl.col("rf"), year=(pl.col("d") // 10000).cast(pl.Int32))
    .group_by("permno", "year")
    .agg(nobs=pl.len(), beta=pl.cov("rx", "mktrf") / pl.col("mktrf").var())
    .filter(pl.col("nobs") >= 200)
    .select("permno", "year", "beta")
    .collect()
)
beta.write_parquet(INTERIM / "beta.parquet")

3.2 Market Capitalization
\[
MktCap_{i,t} = \frac{|ALTPRC_{i,t}| \times SHROUT_{i,t}}{1000}
\]
from the December row of the CRSP monthly file, in millions of dollars. ALTPRC rather than PRC keeps a price when there is no month-end trade; the absolute value removes CRSP’s negative-sign flag for bid–ask midpoints; dividing by 1000 converts thousands of shares × dollars into millions.
msf = pl.read_parquet(RAW / "msf.parquet").with_columns(d=ymd("date"))
msf = msf.with_columns(ym=pl.col("d") // 100, year=(pl.col("d") // 10000).cast(pl.Int32))

    .with_columns(mktcap=pl.col("altprc").abs() * pl.col("shrout") / 1000)
    .filter(pl.col("mktcap") > 0)
    .with_columns(size=pl.col("mktcap").log())
    .select("permno", "year", "altprc", "shrout", "mktcap", "size")
)

title: Chapter 2 — Summary Statistics
text:
3.4 One-Year-Ahead Excess Return
\(r_{i,t+1}\) is the stock’s return over year \(t+1\) minus the risk-free return over year \(t+1\), in percent, attached to the year-\(t\) observation. The book states the monthly return rules explicitly; the annual aggregation is an implementation choice documented here.

Timing
Annual returns are built by return year (ryear) and shifted back one year before the merge, year = ryear - 1, so the 1989 return lands on the 1988 observation. The data end in 2012, so the 2012 cross section has no \(r\) and the Table 2.3 statistics for \(r\) average over 24 years of returns (1989–2012), as the book notes.


Delisting Adjustment
Chapter 7, Section 7.2:







Month
Return used




Ordinary month
CRSP RET


Delisting month, DLRET available
DLRET


Delisting month, DLRET missing, DLSTCD in {500, 520, 551–573, 574, 580, 584}
−30%


Delisting month, DLRET missing, other DLSTCD
−100%









ImportantReplacement, not compounding



The book “take[s] the return of the stock to be the delisting return,” so the delisting month’s return is replaced, not compounded as \((1+RET)(1+DLRET)-1\).


BAD = pl.col("dlstcd").is_in([500, 520, 574, 580, 584]) | pl.col("dlstcd").is_between(551, 573)
dl = (
    pl.read_parquet(RAW / "msedelist.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("dlstcd") > 199)
    .with_columns(ym=ymd("dlstdt") // 100)
    .with_columns(
        dlfill=pl.when(pl.col("dlret").is_not_null()).then(pl.col("dlret"))
               .when(BAD).then(-0.30).otherwise(-1.00),
        how=pl.when(pl.col("dlret").is_not_null()).then(pl.lit("dlret"))
            .when(BAD).then(pl.lit("-30%")).otherwise(pl.lit("-100%")),
    )
    .select("permno", "ym", "dlfill", "how")
)

monthly = (
    msf.select("permno", "ym", "ret")
    .join(dl, on=["permno", "ym"], how="full", coalesce=True)
    .with_columns(
        r=pl.coalesce("dlfill", "ret"),
        both=pl.col("dlfill").is_not_null() & pl.col("ret").is_not_null(),
        ryear=(pl.col("ym") // 100).cast(pl.Int32),
    )
)
msedelist carries a row for every security, with DLSTCD = 100 for those still listed; excluding those rows prevents every surviving stock from receiving a −100% “delisting” return in December 2012. The how column only feeds the diagnostics in Section 8.


Annual Compounding
\[
R^{stock}_{i,t+1} = \prod_{m=1}^{12}(1 + R_{i,m}) - 1,
\qquad
R^{f}_{t+1} = \prod_{m=1}^{12}(1 + RF_{m}) - 1,
\qquad
r_{i,t+1} = 100\,\bigl(R^{stock}_{i,t+1} - R^{f}_{t+1}\bigr).
\]
VALID = pl.col("r").is_finite().fill_null(False)

annual = (
    monthly.filter(pl.col("ryear").is_between(START + 1, END))
    .group_by("permno", "ryear")
    .agg(
        gross=(1 + pl.col("r").filter(VALID)).product(),
        nmon=VALID.sum(),
        ngap=(~VALID).sum(),
        how=pl.col("how").drop_nulls().first(),
        both=pl.col("both").any(),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("ngap") == 0)
)

ffm = pl.read_parquet(RAW / "ff_monthly.parquet").with_columns(ryear=(ymd("date") // 10000).cast(pl.Int32))
rf_annual = (
    ffm.filter(pl.col("ryear").is_between(START + 1, END))
    .group_by("ryear").agg(rf=(1 + pl.col("rf")).product() - 1)
)

r = (
    annual.join(rf_annual, on="ryear")
    .with_columns(r=(pl.col("gross") - 1 - pl.col("rf")) * 100, year=(pl.col("ryear") - 1).cast(pl.Int32))
    .select("permno", "year", "r", "gross", "rf", "nmon", "how", "both")
)
r.write_parquet(INTERIM / "r.parquet")
Two choices the book leaves open: a stock that delists during \(t+1\) is compounded from January to the delisting month, since its monthly rows end there; and a missing RET in an ordinary month makes the annual return missing (ngap == 0) rather than being filled with 0%, following the Chapter 1 rule that an observation is dropped when a required value is unavailable.

title: Chapter 2 — Summary Statistics
text:
3.5 Book-to-Market
\(BM_{i,t} = BE / MktCap\) with book equity from Chapter 10, Section 10.1, following Fama and French (1992, 1993):
\[
BE = SEQ + TXDB + ITCB - PS .
\]







Rule (Chapter 10)
Implementation




Stockholders’ equity SEQ, plus deferred taxes TXDB and investment tax credit ITCB
SEQ + TXDB + ITCB


Preferred stock PS: redemption value, else liquidating value, else par value; zero if all missing
coalesce(PSTKRV, PSTKL, PSTK), fill_null(0)


SEQ or TXDB missing → BE not calculated; ITCB missing → zero
Rows with null SEQ or TXDB dropped; ITCB filled with 0


Compustat format: INDL / STD
Book’s conditions, imposed in the Chapter 1 query. consol = 'C' and popsrc = 'D' are added there as well, to keep one row per firm/date in the current WRDS funda layout


Year \(y\) = calendar year of the fiscal year-end (DATADATE); if two fiscal years end in the same calendar year, use the later one
Group by gvkey, year; keep the last DATADATE


BE from the fiscal year ending in \(y\) over MktCap at the end of December of \(y\)
Join on permno, year with the MktCap table


The ratio computed from year-\(y\) data is treated as known from June of \(y+1\) through May of \(y+2\)
The year-\(t\) observation (December 31 of \(t\)) receives the ratio computed from \(y = t-1\): the data year is shifted forward by one


Link Compustat to CRSP with the CCM link-used table: ULINKTYPE LU or LC, USEDFLAG 1, DATADATE within ULINKDT–ULINKENDDT
First pass


For firms not matched, match CRSP NCUSIP to the first 8 characters of Compustat CUSIP, with DATADATE inside the CRSP name-record interval
Second pass



funda = pl.read_parquet(RAW / "funda.parquet").with_columns(d=ymd("datadate"))
be = (
    funda.filter(pl.col("seq").is_not_null() & pl.col("txdb").is_not_null())
    .with_columns(
        year=(pl.col("d") // 10000).cast(pl.Int32),
        be=pl.col("seq") + pl.col("txdb") + pl.col("itcb").fill_null(0.0)
           - pl.coalesce("pstkrv", "pstkl", "pstk").fill_null(0.0),
    )
    .sort("gvkey", "year", "d")
    .group_by("gvkey", "year", maintain_order=True).last()
    .select("gvkey", "year", "d", "cusip", "be")
)

ccm_path = RAW / "ccm_lnkused.parquet"
if ccm_path.exists():
    lu = (
        pl.read_parquet(ccm_path)
        .filter(pl.col("ulinktype").is_in(["LU", "LC"]) & (pl.col("usedflag") == 1))
        .with_columns(permno=pl.col("upermno").cast(pl.Int64), l0=ymd("ulinkdt"), l1=ymd("ulinkenddt").fill_null(99991231))
        .select(pl.col("ugvkey").alias("gvkey"), "permno", "l0", "l1")
        .drop_nulls("permno")
    )
    via_ccm = (
        be.join(lu, on="gvkey")
        .filter((pl.col("l0") <= pl.col("d")) & (pl.col("d") <= pl.col("l1")))
        .select("gvkey", "permno", "year", "be")
        .with_columns(src=pl.lit("ccm"))
    )
else:
    via_ccm = be.select("gvkey", "permno", "year", "be").clear().with_columns(src=pl.lit("ccm"))

via_cusip = (
    be.join(via_ccm.select("gvkey", "year"), on=["gvkey", "year"], how="anti")
    .with_columns(cusip8=pl.col("cusip").str.slice(0, 8))
    .join(names.select("permno", "ncusip", d0=ymd("namedt"), d1=ymd("nameendt").fill_null(99991231)),
          left_on="cusip8", right_on="ncusip")
    .filter((pl.col("d0") <= pl.col("d")) & (pl.col("d") <= pl.col("d1")))
    .select("gvkey", "permno", "year", "be")
    .with_columns(src=pl.lit("cusip"))
)

bm = (
    pl.concat([via_ccm, via_cusip])
    .unique(subset=["permno", "year"], keep="first", maintain_order=True)
    .join(mktcap.select("permno", "year", "mktcap"), on=["permno", "year"])
    .with_columns(bm=pl.col("be") / pl.col("mktcap"))
    .with_columns(y=pl.col("year"), year=(pl.col("year") + 1).cast(pl.Int32))
    .select("permno", "year", "y", "be", "mktcap", "bm", "src")
)
bs = sample.join(bm, on=["permno", "year"], how="inner")
      f"(link via CCM {bs.filter(pl.col('src') == 'ccm').height:,}, via CUSIP {bs.filter(pl.col('src') == 'cusip').height:,}; "
      f"negative BE {bs.filter(pl.col('be') < 0).height:,} kept)")
bm.write_parquet(INTERIM / "bm.parquet")

title: Chapter 3 — Correlation
text:
Chapter 2 described each variable on its own. Chapter 3 asks how the variables relate to one another, which is usually the actual object of a study. The tool is the cross-sectional correlation, computed with the same two-step logic as the summary statistics: a correlation is calculated within each year’s cross section, and the annual correlations are then averaged over time. The book reports two measures for every pair of variables, the Pearson product–moment correlation, which measures linear association, and the Spearman rank correlation, which measures monotonic association.
This page computes both measures for every pair of \(\beta\), \(Size\), \(BM\), and \(r_{t+1}\) from the stock-year variables that ch02.py stored in data/interim/, and reproduces Table 3.1 (annual correlations), Table 3.2 (their time-series averages), and Table 3.3 (the correlation matrix). All computation happens in this document; the rendered HTML embeds its own resources and can be read on its own.

title: Chapter 3 — Correlation
text:
1.1 Step 1: Cross-Sectional Correlations in Year \(t\)
For each year \(t\) and each pair of variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the calculation uses only the stocks that have valid values of both variables in that year; \(n_t\) is the number of such stocks.
Pearson product–moment correlation. With \(\bar X_t\) and \(\bar Y_t\) the means over those \(n_t\) stocks,
\[
\rho_t(X, Y) =
\frac{\sum_{i}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)}
     {\sqrt{\sum_{i}(X_{i,t}-\bar X_t)^2}\;\sqrt{\sum_{i}(Y_{i,t}-\bar Y_t)^2}} .
\]
Before the Pearson correlation is computed, both variables are winsorized at the 0.5% level, year by year, using only the stocks that enter the pair. Winsorization limits the influence of a handful of extreme observations on a statistic that is sensitive to them.
Spearman rank correlation. Each stock is ranked on \(X\) and on \(Y\) among the same \(n_t\) stocks, with tied values receiving the average of the positions they occupy. With \(d_{i,t} = \text{rank}(X_{i,t}) - \text{rank}(Y_{i,t})\),
\[
\rho^S_t(X, Y) = 1 - \frac{6 \sum_i d_{i,t}^2}{n_t\,(n_t^2 - 1)} .
\]
The rank correlation depends only on orderings, so it is not winsorized: clipping the tails would not change any rank.

title: Chapter 3 — Correlation
text:
1.2 Step 2: Time-Series Average
\[
\rho(X, Y) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t} \rho_t(X, Y),
\qquad
\rho^S(X, Y) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t} \rho^S_t(X, Y),
\]
where \(N\) is the number of years with a valid annual correlation. The result is the correlation in the average year, not the correlation of the pooled panel.






NoteImplementation choices



The book says “winsorized at the 0.5% level”; this page clips each variable at its 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles within the year (0.5% in each tail), the convention used for the Part II analyses. The Spearman correlation is computed with the book’s \(d^2\) formula on average ranks. With ties, this differs slightly from the Pearson correlation of the ranks; for these variables the ties are few enough that the two agree to two decimals.

title: Chapter 4 — Persistence Analysis
text:
Many variables in empirical asset pricing are meant to capture a persistent characteristic of a firm. Beta is the standard example: it is estimated from a year of historical returns on the assumption that the stock’s exposure to the market is reasonably stable, so that the historical estimate says something about the exposure going forward. Chapter 4 introduces a simple check of that assumption, which the book calls persistence analysis: the cross-sectional correlation between a variable measured at time \(t\) and the same variable measured \(\tau\) periods later. A high correlation means the cross-sectional ordering of firms on the variable survives the passage of time; a low one means it does not, either because the characteristic itself changes or because the variable measures it poorly.
This page applies the procedure to \(\beta\), \(Size\), and \(BM\) at lags of one to five years, using the stock-year variables that ch02.py stored in data/interim/, and reproduces Table 4.1 (annual persistence of \(\beta\)), Table 4.2 (its time-series average), and Table 4.3 (average persistence of all three variables). All computation happens in this document.

title: Chapter 4 — Persistence Analysis
text:
1.1 Step 1: Cross-Sectional Persistence in Year \(t\)
For a variable \(X\), a lag \(\tau\), and a year \(t\) such that both \(t\) and \(t+\tau\) lie in the sample period, take every stock \(i\) with a valid value of \(X\) in both years. With \(n_{t,\tau}\) such stocks and means taken over them,
\[
\rho_{t,t+\tau}(X) =
\frac{\sum_i (X_{i,t} - \bar X_t)(X_{i,t+\tau} - \bar X_{t+\tau})}
     {\sqrt{\sum_i (X_{i,t} - \bar X_t)^2}\;\sqrt{\sum_i (X_{i,t+\tau} - \bar X_{t+\tau})^2}} .
\]
This is the Pearson correlation of Chapter 3 applied to one variable at two dates. Before it is computed, the year-\(t\) values and the year-\((t+\tau)\) values are each winsorized at the 0.5% level, separately, over the stocks that enter the calculation.

title: Chapter 4 — Persistence Analysis
text:
1.2 Step 2: Time-Series Average
\[
\rho_{\tau}(X) = \frac{1}{N_\tau} \sum_t \rho_{t,t+\tau}(X),
\]
where \(N_\tau\) is the number of years for which the lag-\(\tau\) correlation exists. The book calls \(\rho_\tau(X)\) the persistence of \(X\) at lag \(\tau\). With a sample ending in 2012, the last year with a lag-1 value is 2011 and the last with a lag-5 value is 2007, so \(N_\tau = 25 - \tau\).






NoteImplementation choice



“Winsorized at the 0.5% level” is implemented as clipping at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles (0.5% in each tail), year by year, computed on the stocks that have both values. The two dates are winsorized independently, as the book specifies.
